Rock-n-Roll Yoga is really a good class. Or maybe it's that Natalie (Martina? Nikola? Sorry, I don't remember) is a good teacher. Good voice, good rhythm. The rock-n-roll part wasn't as rockin' as I'd hoped, but that's ok, it was still fun. 45 minutes, great for a vacation-sized class. I'd give the class 3 stars, but it gets 4 because of the aweeeesome locker room which is super convenient for going to class then changing and going to the pool. All in all, a good experience!

Lounge with lazyboy-type chairs; check. Television; check. Roberto's and Pinkbox Doughnuts; check, check. Coconut water for merely 2 (.5 liter); check. What more does one require? I have never gotten a car washed here (and probably never will). I do not purchase petro here (it appears to be obscenely overpriced). And I do not care for motor oil changes. The staff is friendly, the convenience of the location optimal for anyone frequenting the RTC Park Ride, and since there is hardly anything else remaining to be stated: I am a fan. - E Postscript. There are PC terminals in the lounge as well. Never used them but I have noticed children playing on them, so I am sure they work. YMMV.

I have lived in Las Vegas for about 4 years and this was by far the best meal I have had here. The service, food and wine were excellent. Hugo's Cellar is an old school dining experience. It is like going back in a time machine to how things used to be. The salad cart was an impressive and unexpected addition to a wonderful steak. Both steaks were cooked perfectly and had a seasoning that matched the meat well. We dined late so we only waited about 10-15 minutes but if you want to visit during peak hours I advise making reservations.

Uber should be allowed to operate in a city regardless of whether it is willing to follow the same (or comparable) regulations as the city's regular taxis. The regulations governing taxis may not necessarily be in the best interests of residents or visitors, and they may not reflect the changing needs of an evolving city. Allowing Uber to operate without some of these regulations would still ensure that riders have safe, reliable, and affordable transportation options, while allowing for innovation and flexibility that may benefit both riders and drivers. Furthermore, Uber has shown a willingness to comply with local regulations wherever it operates, so allowing it to operate in a city without having to adhere to existing taxi regulations might only result in a better outcome for everyone involved.

As a society we have limited resources. We have to decide how to best use those resources. Spending thousands of dollars on a child that is unlikely to recover is not the right way, but what would be? It's hard for me to say because I don't know exactly what happened in this case and am speculating based on other cases (it also costs more than 25k). And she wasn't sent home - they removed her from life support while still inside the hospital where she was being treated. She died there after having been declared brain dead by both doctors family members themselves before even getting transferred out.

The George W. Bush years may be perceived as a dark age in world history by some, but not all. Many people believe that the Bush years were a time of great progress and accomplishment, both domestically and internationally. Bush was a strong leader who made tough decisions in difficult times, and his legacy will be one of a president who kept America safe and made the world a better place.

Fiction merely provides entertainment. It doesn't help us grow at all. There are other sources of information that help us grow much better. If that is so, what is the point in reading fiction? Is life not a story? I don't think we can just say "this is true and this isn't." One could argue that there's no truth because there's no one way to interpret something but rather interpretations based off of our experiences, backgrounds, etc...

While everyone is entitled to their own opinion, there are several reasons why hardcore punk music is actually far from boring. First, one of the defining characteristics of punk music is its raw and energetic sound, which often includes fast-paced guitar riffs and aggressive drumming that can be incredibly invigorating to listen to. Additionally, the themes explored in many hardcore punk songs, such as social and political injustice, personal struggles, and rebellion against authority, can be deeply relatable and impactful to listeners. Finally, the DIY ethos and community-driven nature of punk culture can provide a sense of belonging and purpose to those who participate in it. Therefore, it is important to recognize that while hardcore punk may not be to everyone's taste, it can still hold significant value and meaning for those who enjoy it.

I don't think anyone wants to see violence directed towards members of another racial group; however, why should we not act on statements made by one person toward others because of their race, either through verbal abuseharassment or even worse? For example: You're black, therefore all blacks must work twice as hard just to get half as far. Or my personal favorite: Oh yeah, I'm going home after class today. If a parent says something along those lines to his child, and he does not teach him otherwise, then yes, the kid will learn from this and grow into a racist adult himself. Same applies to kids being taught that only whites are superior. So what am I saying? People say and write things without thinking them out very well. This leads us down some pretty dangerous paths. Supporting higher learning for both teachers AND students alike is crucial for the future of America.

Arthritis is inflammation of the joints. Arthritis comes in well over 100 different forms, from genetic disorders, to viral infections, to the result of physical trauma. Anyone at any age can get arthritis. The most common form is osteoarthritis, which affects about 80 of people over 65 years old. The exact cause of osteoarthritis (OA) remains unknown. There are various theories as to what causes OA; however, there's no cure or proven way to prevent it. What can I do if I have symptoms? If you have pain and stiffness in your knees, hips, back, neck andor shoulder, talk with a health care provider right away. You may be prescribed medication for milder cases of joint pain and swelling. If the problem isn't improving after several weeks, you should see an orthopedic physician who specializes in treating arthritis. Even though some studies show that exercise does help relieve knee osteoarthritis pain, you shouldn't try this without consulting a medical professional first. In many cases, exercising too much could make things worse instead of better. Start out slowly by warming up, stretching and strengthening your muscles before beginning an activity like walking. How soon will my joints hurt less or go away completely? It's impossible to predict how quickly relief might come. Sometimes, depending on where you're hurting, it takes only two days to start feeling better. Other times, even minor daily activities can seem painful. Keeping active helps control pain, muscle spasms and stiffness. Exercise also strengthens bones, ligaments and tendons so they don't become weaker over time.

Understanding E3 ligase and target substrate interactions are important for cell biology and therapeutic development. However, experimental identification of E3 target relationships is not an easy task due to the complexity of the pathways and the large number of potential targets. One approach to identifying E3-substrate interactions is through the use of proteomics technology, which allows for the identification of protein-protein interactions within a cellular context. This can be coupled with gene knockdown or overexpression techniques to investigate the effects of altered E3 levels on substrate protein ubiquitination. Other methods include the use of substrate trapping mutants, which contain an inactive E3 ligase domain and a substrate-binding domain, allowing for the isolation of E3-substrate complexes. Additionally, the use of small molecule inhibitors or peptidomimetics that disrupt E3-substrate interactions can be used to identify and study these protein-protein interactions.

Crowd counting from unconstrained scene images is a crucial task in many real-world applications like urban surveillance and management, but it is greatly challenged by the camera's perspective that causes depth distortions. We address this problem by combining three datasets: (i) an interactive reconstruction of the scene at two viewpoints using stereo images; (ii) immersive 3D world models in which the objects are modeled as point clouds without any textures or details; (iii) a set of robust and accurate sensor calibration methods to estimate the camera parameters such as geometric shape and distance to its object targets. Our approach provides efficient feature learning for sparse cloud representations and enables accurate estimation of unknown camera parameters with high accuracy through calibration. We show that our method retains the advantages compared to other convolutional approaches while outperforming them in terms of data handling and speed when used on large datasets. Language: en

We consider a wireless distributed computing system, in which multiple mobile users, connected wirelessly through an access point, collaborate to perform a computation task. In particular, users communicate with each other using the wireless network andor one or more applications running on client devices within this wireless distributed computing environment. Distributed systems can be implemented by any number of hardware platforms, for example computer servers that are configured according to certain operating procedures and software components installed thereon (e.g., telemetry-receiving subsystems). Distributed computers may also include networks such as local area networks (LAN) and wide area networks (WAN), which connect nodes together over physical distances. In order to function efficiently, these types of networks need to maintain data integrity between the various nodes. Data integrity is maintained when every node has access to all information stored at another node, but only after the data has been checked against checksums, signed with public keys, etc. A problem commonly encountered during real time communications among many users involves several users transmitting information simultaneously across the same connection or across different connections. For instance, if two people are conducting simultaneous telephone calls via cellular phones they will both send their voice messages. During transmission, some packets may be lost because of interference from other packets being transmitted along the same link or scheduled for transmission later. Other losses occur due to reflections off buildings, walls, etc. One solution used today to lessen the effects caused by collisions is to "collision detect" - i.e., sending a collision detection packet in response to detecting a collision; however, there might not always be enough available bandwidth to transmit this type of large packet quickly. Another solution to diminish the effect of colliding traffic would be to use a smaller packet size, thereby reducing the amount of overhead needed to transfer it. A third way to reduce the problems associated with collisions could involve congestion avoidance. Conventional solutions suffer from either poor performance compared to their theoretical counterparts, requiring too much processor resources, possible signal distortion, or high latency responses. Hence, a need exists for methods and apparatus that provide a simple mechanism for minimizing the impact of collisions without sacrificing throughput or processing efficiency.

We study the problem of recognizing visual entities from the textual descriptions of their classes. Specifically, given birds' images with free-text descriptions of their species, we learn to classify images as belonging either to a particular class or not by using machine learning methods such as support vector machines and deep neural networks (DNNs). Our approach is based on three main steps: 1) extract features automatically for each image; 2) build an auto-encoder network in which one layer encodes pairs of words into other information that may be used later while training DNN models; 3) perform preprocessing tasks like feature normalization prior to feeding low level image features to feedforward and backpropagation layers within DNN model. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness through several experiments using different datasets collected at various locations across Israel including BirdLife International's global checklist database.

We present a local routing algorithm which guarantees delivery in all connected graphs embedded on a known surface of genus g. The algorithm transports O (g log n) memory and runs in O (n log n) time, where n is the number of nodes in the graph. This algorithm is particularly useful in wireless mesh networks, where nodes may have limited memory and processing power. By guaranteeing delivery in all connected graphs embedded on a known surface of genus g, the algorithm ensures that messages will be reliably transmitted across the network without requiring excessive resources. Additionally, the algorithm's runtime and memory requirements are logarithmic in the size of the graph, making it scalable for large networks. Overall, this local routing algorithm is a valuable tool for optimizing communication in wireless mesh networks and other graph-based systems.

We propose a novel regularization-based continual learning method, dubbed as Adaptive Group Sparsity based Continual Learning (AGS-CL), using two group sparsity-based penalties. Our method selectively employs the two penalties when discovering a new feature in order to model the optimal relationship between the features and their respective classes. This is achieved by means of a regularized nonlinear least squares optimization framework which allows us to find an optimized solution for each class. We apply AGS-CL on an image segmentation task with multiple features per object instance. The results show that our method not only outperforms other existing methods but also exhibits significant improvements compared to baseline methods without any prior knowledge about the data set. Synergistic interactions are ubiquitous in the real world. Recent studies have revealed that, for a single-layer network, synergy can enhance spreading and even induce an explosive contagion. There is at least one universal property of real-world networks that is known to promote synergy: the existence of mesoscale modules or communities. We study the effect of modularity on synergistic interactions, and show that modular structure can strongly enhance the synergy-driven spreading. Specifically, we find that the synergy-driven spreading threshold decreases with increasing modularity, and can even become zero in certain cases. We also find that the synergy-driven contagion exhibits a discontinuous transition from subcritical to supercritical when the modularity exceeds a certain critical value. Our findings demonstrate that modular structure can significantly amplify synergy-induced contagion, and suggest that modularity may be an important factor for understanding the emergence of explosive epidemics in the real world.

The current gold standard for human activity recognition (HAR) is based on the use of cameras. However, the poor scalability of camera systems renders them impractical in pursuit of the following goals: mass adoption at both low- and high-cost points; robustness to environmental changes such as weather conditions or lighting variations; long battery life with minimal maintenance requirements; and ease of integration into existing infrastructure. In this work, we build a generic architecture of Convolutional Neural Networks to discover empirical properties of neural networks. Our first contribution is to introduce a state-of-the-art framework that depends only on the output and training inputs of a standard convolutional network (e.g., an LSTM). We show how these two parameters can be extracted from a trained model via a novel feature extraction algorithm for supervised classification. This approach permits us to efficiently use off-line data in learning, while still maintaining a desirable level of accuracy when running on real-time data streams. We then combine our abstract classifier with a deep recurrent neural network to learn a new type of model capable of making predictions about unseen data streams. The resulting representation captures similarities between different classes by generating vector representations of trained samples. It also captures dissimilarities between those same classes by constructing vectors representing unlabeled samples and comparing them to one another over time. In addition, it learns discriminative features such as edges, lines or curves that are used for both classification and regression tasks. We demonstrate that this representation has excellent performance across several artificial intelligence tasks including image recognition, language translation, and object detection.

This paper deals with a complete bipartite matching problem with the objective of finding an optimal matching that maximizes a certain generic predefined utility function on the set of all possible matchings. In order to solve this problem, several algorithms have been proposed over the years, including the Hungarian algorithm, the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm, and the augmenting path algorithm. The Hungarian algorithm is a well-known algorithm that solves the bipartite matching problem in polynomial time. It works by starting with an empty matching and iteratively adding edges to the matching until a maximum matching is obtained. The algorithm uses a clever method called the Hungarian method to identify augmenting paths in the graph, which are paths alternating between matched and unmatched edges. The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm is another well-known algorithm that also solves the bipartite matching problem in polynomial time. It utilizes a breadth-first search approach to find augmenting paths in the graph. The algorithm performs a series of alternating breadth-first searches, starting at unmatched vertices in one bipartition and moving towards unmatched vertices in the other bipartition. The algorithm terminates when no more augmenting paths can be found. The augmenting path algorithm is an algorithm that also solves the bipartite matching problem in polynomial time. It works by finding augmenting paths in the graph and iteratively updating the matching until a maximum matching is obtained. The algorithm uses a technique called depth-first search to find augmenting paths in the graph. All of these algorithms have been proven to be efficient in solving the bipartite matching problem. The choice of algorithm depends on various factors, such as the size of the graph and the specific application.

We present and analyze a numerical method to solve the time-dependent linear Pauli equation in three space-dimensions. The Pauli equation is a "semi-relativistic" generalization of the Schrodinger equation for 2-spinors , which has its roots in quantum mechanics but can also be formulated as an ordinary differential equation describing heat transport or particle collisions on curved surfaces at high speed. Our approach involves two iterative schemes: firstly we use elliptic boundary conditions; secondly, using integer solutions obtained by solving this equation numerically with an expectation value problem (EVP). We compare our EVP scheme against existing techniques based either upon evolution equations or Newton's method [1]. In particular, it outperforms conventional methods when applied to problems involving strongly nonlinear terms such as diffusion coefficients where exponential decay rates are inherent properties that cannot be ignored. Moreover, unlike standard Newtonian algorithms employed up until now, ours do not require explicit knowledge about partial derivatives between variables involved into iteration computations - the computational cost consequently decreases drastically compared to other approaches due to the reduced need for calculation accuracy beyond unity during every step toward convergence."

Despite being the standard loss function to train multi-class neural networks, the log-softmax has two potential limitations. First, it involves computations that scale linearly with the number of output classes, which can become computationally expensive as the number of classes increases. Second, the log-softmax function is sensitive to outliers, which can misrepresent the loss function and degrade model performance. To address these limitations, some alternatives to the log-softmax function have been proposed, such as the focal loss function, which down-weights the contribution of easy examples, and the sparsemax function, which encourages sparsity in the predicted probabilities. Other approaches include the hierarchical softmax and adaptive softmax, which reduce the computational cost of computing the loss function in large output spaces.

Recent years have seen big advances in the field of sentence-level quality estimation (QE), largely as a result of using neural-based architectures. However, the majority of these methods work only on sentence-level data and do not take discourse-level information into account. In this paper, we present a novel neural-based QE system that uses discourse-level information to identify and correct errors in long text documents. Our method employs a hierarchical recurrent neural network (HRNN) to capture both sentence-level and discourse-level information, and then uses an attention mechanism to focus on the most relevant parts of the text. We evaluate our system on a corpus of student essays annotated with error tags, and show that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems. We further analyze the system's performance on different types of errors, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting both grammar and style errors. Our results suggest that incorporating discourse-level information can lead to more accurate predictions of sentence-level quality, and give promising directions for future work.

The fuzzy K -means problem is a generalization of the classical K -means problem to soft clusterings, i.e. clusterings where each points belongs to each cluster to some degree. Although the classical K -means problem is NP-hard, it has been shown that the fuzzy K -means problem can be solved efficiently in polynomial time. The fuzzy K -means problem is defined as follows: Given a set of n points S and an integer k , find a partition of S into k clusters such that the sum of the squared distances between each point and the centroid of its cluster is minimized. A solution to the fuzzy K -means problem is a partition of S into k clusters, where each cluster is defined by a set of points and a centroid. The centroid of a cluster is the average of all points in the cluster.

Importance of visual context in scene understanding tasks is well recognized in the computer vision community. However, to what extent the computer vision models for image classification and semantic segmentation are dependent on this contextual information has not been explored so far. In order to understand whether a given model can handle large-scale environmental changes such as object occlusions or lighting changes it is important that we can evaluate our models' performance under these challenging scenarios by exposing them to real world data sets containing near simultaneously captured images from different locations with different backgrounds. Realworld workspaces contain multiple static scenes including objects, which generally have similar color and texture properties. The appearance of each object differs only slightly due to variations in illumination conditions (in terms of intensity and spectral composition), object orientation and viewpoint. Such changeable environmental factors have significant impact on our ability to classify realistic human faces collected over long periods of time cite28, as do the differences between individuals cite26. Visual similarities may also be masked by global camera pose transformations cite3, thus augmenting existing spatial invariant cues must help us better resolve these issues. This is particularly relevant when dealing with pedestrian detection in urban areas where we need high recall rates while having enough resolution to distinguish pedestrians from cars, bicyclists, motorcycles, etc even though they all typically share similar appearances under normal light conditions cite5.

We study the problem of recognizing visual entities from the textual descriptions of their classes. Specifically, given birds' images with free-text descriptions of their species, we learn to classify images into one of the classes. Since the descriptions can vary significantly in length and content, we propose a model to learn representations of visual entities by extracting relevant information from the text without relying on any hand-crafted features. Our approach is based on an encoder-decoder architecture, where the encoder maps the textual description into a latent embedding space. The decoder takes both the embedding and the image as input and predicts the class label. We evaluate our proposed method on the challenging Birdsnap dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results. Our method follows an encoder-decoder architecture, which consists of two main modules: the encoder and the decoder. The encoder module is responsible for mapping the given textual description into a latent embedding space. This is done by leveraging a pre-trained language model (e.g., BERT) to extract meaningful information from the text. The decoder takes both the embedding and the image as input and predicts the class label. To train our model, we use a cross-entropy loss with regularization terms to ensure the smoothness of the latent embedding space and its consistency with the original text. We evaluate our method on the challenging Birdsnap dataset, a collection of images of birds with free-text descriptions of their species. We compare our results with several baseline methods and show that our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art results on this task. In particular, our method outperforms the baselines by a significant margin, with an accuracy of 86.9.

Meanwhile, the reconstructed version (which corresponds to the output from the synthesizer) is also made available as a reference against which the discriminator also tries to fool it. The final output is thus the "realistic" match score, which accounts for various factors such as facial appearance, texture changes, etc., of older individuals. We use GAN based approach since it provides efficient training procedure and can produce high quality results even when trained on very low-quality data with limited examples. The analysis techniques of system log messages (syslog messages) have a long history from when the syslog mechanism was invented. Typically, the analysis consists of two parts, one is a static analysis and the other is a dynamic analysis. The static analysis consists of analyzing system log messages, without any context-based information, to detect known attack patterns. There are several approaches to performing this type of analysis, including simple statistical methods and more sophisticated data mining techniques. The dynamic analysis consists of analyzing system log messages together with other context information (e.g., user behavior) to detect attacks. In this paper, we focus on the static analysis of system log messages for security purposes. There are several challenges in analyzing system log messages for security purposes. One is that system log messages are typically unstructured text, which makes it difficult to extract useful information from them. Another challenge is that system log messages can be generated by different devices and software applications, which can lead to a large number of different message formats. This can make it difficult to develop a single analysis approach that can be used for all messages. Finally, system log messages can be generated by both legitimate and malicious activity, which can make it difficult to distinguish between the two. In this paper, we survey existing approaches for analyzing system log messages for security purposes. We categorize these approaches into five main categories: rule-based approaches, statistical approaches, data mining approaches, hybrid approaches, and visualization approaches. For each category, we discuss the main methods that have been proposed and evaluate their strengths and weaknesses. We also discuss some of the challenges that remain in this area.

Recent studies have shown that the environment where people eat can affect their nutritional behaviour. In this work, we provide automatic tools for personalised analysis of a person's health habits and food choices through their mobile phone. A typical day in our offices is filled with data collection from hundreds of users throughout the country. The purpose of all these was to help us better understand key behaviours linked to health - such as who is eating what type of food at home or how much fruit they are consuming. We then use those information feeds high-speed internet connections to analyse patterns across many different scenarios. Our goal is to identify trends and predict whether certain behaviour changes are driven by lifestyle factors like spending time outside and physical activity. In order to make a predictive model - using artificial intelligence technology - it has become necessary to be able to track multiple points on a person's life over time to translate into an understanding of the trajectory of a disease. That is why we developed the life span score system (LSS), which aims to do just that. The LSS measures several health aspects which influence appetite - including age, sex, family history and weight. When combined with medical markers - such as blood pressure, body mass index and cholesterol levels - it provides a more accurate picture of risk for specific diseases. It also identifies fluctuations in dietary intake during periods associated with illness and chronic conditions such as heart disease, diabetes, stroke, cancer, depression, anxiety, smoking disorder etc., thus allowing for rapid prediction of future disease trajectories. Healthcare providers rely heavily on these predictions to determine treatment options for patients based on both clinical observations and historical records. However, they don't always offer sufficient insight into long-term relationships between diet and health outcomes due to limited knowledge about the effect of diet on health overall. One solution could be device integration into existing healthcare infrastructure supporting free mobile access. This would allow individualisation of interventions that target specific issues within the population. We hope that our research will contribute to providing valuable insights into our current world, and lead towards the development of novel approaches to improve human health.

The UK's economic woes reflect in part some long-standing structural problems within British society itself: stagnant wages, high unemployment rates for young people (and immigrants), underemployment among many women in jobs that do not fit their skill sets, and an overall lack of confidence on the part of both employers and employees as to the future direction toward which Britain is heading. The response in terms of fiscal policy has been limited and inadequate; austerity measures have been based largely upon further cuts to state spending that will be implemented via a "pay freeze" - often referred to more accurately as pay cuts given the real value erosion of public sector salaries relative to private sector ones since 2008 or so. There was also at least one round of tax increases targeted against those earning 100kyear or more back around 2010 to 2012. But there were no major reforms undertaken with respect to the taxation structure that would have provided adequate revenue streams necessary to support growth in demand from consumers in order to create employment opportunities through investment. What we see instead are reductions in government expenditures that ultimately need to be financed if they are going to achieve any serious results whatsoever. This should come as little surprise given the fact that the austerity approach had never achieved any kind of success throughout history before it became the favored strategy amongst the world's governments during this era. In addition, debt servicing costs seem poised to rise sharply in 2013 due to the maturing of sovereign bonds issued prior to the onset of the financial crisis, putting additional pressure upon already strained budgets.

The Yom Kippur War began with a coordinated surprise attack by Syria and Egypt against Israel on the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur. The war lasted for three weeks and resulted in a significant territorial gain for Syria and Egypt, as well as a major Israeli defeat.

The plague disease, caused by Yersinia pestis, is enzootic (commonly present) in populations of fleas carried by ground rodents, including marmots, in various areas including Central Asia, Kurdistan, Western Asia, and Europe. Infected flea-infested animals are considered most likely to infest domestic and wild mammals, especially livestock (e.g., sheep herds), then infect humans through bite wounds or unwashed hands that come into contact with the infected animal's carcass, soil contaminated with fecal matter from an infected animal, etc. Plague has been eradicated from many countries due to effective public health measures and vaccination programs; however, outbreaks periodically occur worldwide because of the persistence of rodent reservoirs harboring the pathogen. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports a continuous increase heretofore reported year over year since 2015 in the number of human cases of bubonic plague infections reported globally amongst individuals under the age of 20 years - indicating that young persons may be much more vulnerable than previously thought to this life threatening infection. Additionally, and perhaps very importantly, there have been increases in recent years throughout Eurasia in the numbers of isolates of bacteria associated with the occurrence of plague. However, despite these increased incidences of plague, the development of a vaccine against plague remains elusive. In fact, one could argue that even after nearly 30 years since the first successful clinical trials on a live attenuated strain of Y. pestis with respect to the prevention of pneumonic plague, progress toward developing a highly efficacious live recombinant vaccine (bacterial protein antigens) capable of inducing protective immunity in healthy adults has stalled, and no reliable endpoint can currently be predicted as to when plague will be eliminated.

The alga Cyanophora, a glaucophyte, is thought to be one of the first organisms to contain a chloroplast. The glaucophyte chloroplast group is the smallest of the three primary chloroplast groups (see Fig. 2.1). The other two primary groups are the euglenoids and the haptophytes, which are the major representatives of the chlorophyte group. The glaucophytes include the orders Pavlova (Pavlova and Pterocladia, coccoid species) and Cyanidiales (two genera: Cyanidium and Cyanophora). The algae in this group do not have a cell wall, are haploid, and have a chloroplast that has the same morphology as the plastids of the other two primary groups. The plastid stroma is a single layer of flattened thylakoids (the flat folded membranes that have chlorophylls and other pigments) in which there are vesicles that contain starch. The plastid in the euglenoids has a different structure (see Fig. 2.1). Figure 2.2: Chloroplasts from different algal groups. Chloroplasts from (a) a glaucophyte, (b) a euglenoid, and (c) a haptophyte. Studies using molecular and biochemical techniques have shown that the alga Cyanophora is a sister group of all other chlorophytes. Thus, it is possible that the chloroplasts of all the other algae evolved from the chloroplast of Cyanophora. In the glaucophytes, the plastids are distributed throughout the cells rather than being concentrated in the chloroplasts. The plastids in glaucophytes are large, round, and contain a great deal of starch. Starch granules are seen in the lamellae of the stroma of the plastids and are called cisternae (singular: cisterna). Cyanophora is a marine alga that lives in the open sea and is common in the intertidal zone of the Pacific Ocean. It is found in the waters around Japan and is commonly called tetrasiphon (from the Greek words "four" and "vessel.

Reactive oxygen species, such as superoxide ion (O- 2) and hydrogen peroxide (H 2O 2), are dangerous by-products of oxygen use in organisms. Parts of the immune system of higher organisms produce reactive oxygen species to kill invading pathogens. However, excessive or uncontrolled production of these molecules can damage cell structures, including DNA, proteins and phospholipid membranes, and lead to cell death or tissue damage. To counteract the harmful effects of reactive oxygen species, organisms have evolved antioxidant systems that scavenge these molecules and prevent their accumulation. These systems can involve enzymes, such as superoxide dismutase and catalase, that convert reactive oxygen species to less harmful compounds, as well as small molecules, such as glutathione and vitamin C, that can directly react with them and neutralize their reactivity. Knowing the balance between reactive oxygen species and antioxidant defenses is important for understanding many biological processes, such as aging, cancer, and inflammation.

In October 1529, Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse, convoked an assembly of German and Swiss theologians at the Marburg Colloquy, to establish doctrinal unity in the emerging Protestant states. Agreement was reached on the basic Protestant teachings, but tensions arose over the role of the Roman Catholic Church. Convoked by Landgrave Philip of Hesse , the Marburg Colloquy was an attempt to resolve doctrinal disputes among various German Protestant groups. The discussion was held in Marburg on October 27-November 2, 1529. It was attended by a few German Protestant and Swiss Reformers, such as Martin Luther , John Eck , and Melanchthon . The Catholic theologians included Cardinal Cajetan and Johannes Pfefferkorn , a Dominican monk who had collected a large number of forbidden books in Germany and sent them to Rome. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss the Lutheran doctrine of justification. The meeting was convened in order to bring about doctrinal unity among the Protestant groups, which included the Lutherans, the Zwinglians, and the Anabaptists, and to establish the legitimacy of the Protestant movement. The discussion took place between Luther and Cajetan. Melanchthon served as the mediator. The first day was devoted to the question of the scope of the Bible, whether or not only the Old Testament was necessary to establish doctrine, which was one of the main issues of dispute between Luther and Cajetan. The second day was devoted to justification. The third day was spent on the sacraments, and on the fourth and fifth days the other major doctrines of Protestantism were discussed. The Marburg Colloquy was a significant event in the history of the Protestant Reformation because it established the Lutheran view of justification, which became a key component of Protestant doctrine. However, this agreement was short-lived. The Protestant movement was plagued by division and disagreement, and the issue of justification became one of the main points of conflict. Cyanobacteria are considered the ancestors of chloroplasts. They are sometimes called blue-green algae even though they are prokaryotes. They are a diverse phylum of bacteria capable of carrying out photosynthesis, although they are not true plants. Cyanobacteria are unicellular organisms with a distinctive membrane-bound chloroplast, and are the source of oxygen that the Earth has been using for the past 2.6 billion years. They have been classified into three groups: heterocystous, photoheterocystous, and autotrophic. Heterocystous cyanobacteria are usually green in color and do not form chlorophyll. Photoheterocystous cyanobacteria form small colonies of yellow-green cells and can photosynthesize, but do not produce oxygen. Autotrophic cyanobacteria have a chlorophyll-containing chloroplast and can synthesize oxygen. These organisms are able to fix carbon dioxide and produce oxygen. Their photosynthesis is similar to that of chloroplasts, and their stroma lamellae and thylakoids are similar in structure to those of chloroplasts. In some cyanobacteria, the chloroplasts are divided into etioplasts, which lack thylakoids, and leucoplasts, which have thylakoids. The thylakoids are made of the same protein complex as chloroplast thylakoids, but the stroma lamellae contain proteins and pigments that are different from those of chloroplasts.

The Rankine cycle is the fundamental thermodynamic underpinning of the steam engine. The cycle is an arrangement of components as is typically used for simple power production, and utilizes the thermodynamic properties of water to efficiently convert thermal energy into mechanical work. The Rankine cycle consists of four components: an evaporator, a turbine, a condenser, and a pump. Heat is added to the system in the evaporator, where liquid water is heated, vaporized, and then expanded in the turbine. The expanding steam produces mechanical work, which can be used to drive an electrical generator or other machinery. After passing through the turbine, the steam is cooled and condensed in the condenser before returning to the evaporator as liquid via the pump. The Rankine cycle is the basis for most modern power plants, including nuclear and coal-fired power plants.

The Court's decision in that case was appealed by the French government to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which ruled that France's right to family life was inconsistent with Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). The Court also said that there was a conflict between the right to family life and Articles 1, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 of the ECHR. The ECHR's ruling was appealed to the European Court of Justice, which confirmed the ECHR's decision in 2011.

The Mongol Empire was governed by a civilian and military code, called the Yassa, created by Genghis Khan. The Mongol Empire did not emphasize the importance of ethnicity and race , but instead focused on loyalty and merit. The Yassa set out rules for governing the empire, including regulations on taxation, military service, justice, and trade. It also established customs and rituals, such as saluting the Khan by kneeling before him. In addition to the Yassa, Genghis Khan established a decentralized system of administration that gave local leaders considerable independence in running local affairs, while maintaining tight control over foreign policy and military strategy. This decentralized system, known as the "Mongolian System," allowed the Empire to remain united despite its vast size and disparate ethnic composition. The Mongol Empire sought to ensure the loyalty of its subjects through a combination of violence, rewards, and patronage. Genghis Khan was known for his merciless treatment of enemies, but he also rewarded those who were loyal to him with titles, land grants, and other privileges. He placed great emphasis on meritocracy and often promoted people to positions of authority based on their skill and ability rather than their social standing or ethnicity. The Mongol Empire was highly militaristic and maintained a large army composed of soldiers from many different ethnic backgrounds. The army was divided into divisions called tumens, each led by an experienced general. Discipline was strict and punishments harsh, but the army was nevertheless well trained and successful in conquest.

Researchers from the California Institute of Technology have verified a theory that could lead to quantum batteries - a new form of energy storage technology. The breakthrough, published in Nature Materials, revolves around a concept called 'quantum coherence', which is the ability of an electron to maintain its quantum state over a long period of time. The researchers found that it was possible to store electrical charge in a semiconductor material for an extended period without the electrons losing their quantum state. This finding could have profound implications for the development of quantum batteries - a type of energy storage device that would be much more efficient than traditional batteries. The team tested the concept using a nanostructured aluminum oxide film that was placed between two electrodes. When a voltage was applied to the electrodes, the electrons in the film were able to maintain their quantum state for up to one millisecond, which is much longer than the fraction of a nanoseconds it takes for them to lose their quantum state in normal conditions. This proof of concept could pave the way for further research into the development of quantum batteries and other related technologies. "The fact that we can now see that this kind of coherence can last for milliseconds is really important, because now it's worth looking into devices that take advantage of this," said Caltech professor Jelena Vuckovic in a press release. While the research is still in its early stages, the findings could potentially revolutionize the way we store and use energy. If successful, quantum batteries could enable us to create far more efficient energy storage systems than what exists today.

Scientists and engineers have designed a new origami-inspired lunar habitat that has the capability to unfold into 750 times its own size. This achievement comes as a remarkable breakthrough in the field of space exploration and promises new possibilities for future lunar missions. The habitat, called "Lunar Quattro-Hab" was developed by scientists from the Bremen University of Applied Sciences and the German Aerospace Centre. The design aims to provide a more convenient and efficient way to construct lunar settlements. The current process of constructing lunar habitats involves manually erecting rigid, container-like structures on the surface. The Lunar Quattro-Hab is unique because of its ability to pack flat into a container for transport and deployment on the lunar surface. The mechanism uses Origami folds on a lightweight metal frame to unfold and create a super-large structure of thousands of square meters. The design is configured to provide ample space for up to four astronauts to live and conduct scientific experiments for several weeks or months. The research team has tested Lunar Quattro-Hab in simulated lunar environments, and the results have been impressive. The folded structure exhibits versatility and robustness, withstanding extreme temperatures, radiation, and the impact of small meteoroids that commonly hit the moon's surface. The Lunar Quattro-Hab not only carries a spacious habitat but also provides a reliable framework to support the associated logistics of future lunar missions. This innovative achievement represents a significant milestone for space exploration and could indicate new discoveries yet to come. With the Lunar Quattro-Hab, the idea of establishing permanent lunar settlements seems more achievable than ever before. It is hoped that this new design will inspire further research and contribute to creating a sustainable human presence on the moon. The Bremen University of Applied Sciences and the German Aerospace Centre plan to advance Lunar Quattro-Hab to incorporate enhanced technology, including self-sustaining power, and water availability. The researchers expect that their contribution to a rapidly developing space industry will continue to grow as they solve more problems in future space missions.

Scientists at MIT have published a paper detailing a new type of artificial brain synapse that can potentially produce devices that can handle complex AI computing locally without having to send data to the cloud. According to the researchers, the technology could produce "event-based" neuromorphic computing, meaning it could work more efficiently by responding to actual signals instead of having to wait for data to stream through it at a certain rate. The new device is based on the phase-change memory (PCM) already found in many computers, and could be a big step toward bringing AI functions to a wide range of devices. The researchers said that in order for artificial intelligence to work locally on mobile devices, it needs to be able to respond to the unpredictable timing of the signals it receives. The team claims to have accomplished this using PCM - a memory technology that stores data by altering the state of the chalcogenide glass - in a way that allows the glass to undergo sudden changes when electricity is applied to it. By exploiting this sudden change, the PCM can be used to represent the binary states used by conventional computers. But unlike existing technologies, PCMs can be switched back and forth between the two states in less than a trillionth of a second. By combining PCM with a fast-switching transistor, the researchers were able to create a new type of synapse that can be programmed to fire when it receives a specific signal. The researchers were also able to demonstrate that the synapses could be connected together to form a neuromorphic array that was able to perform a simple, unsupervised machine-learning task. The work is currently being patented through the MIT Technology Licensing Office.

Wyoming has made history by approving the first Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) in America. The DAO, called "American CryptoFed DAO," is a new type of organization that is run by its members through code instead of a central authority. The American CryptoFed DAO was created with the aim of creating a stablecoin, a type of cryptocurrency that is pegged to the value of a real-world asset to minimize volatility. The DAO's stablecoin, called "DAC," will be backed by the US dollar, making it a trustworthy and reliable option for cryptocurrency users. The DAO was approved by the Wyoming Secretary of State's office on July 1st, 2021, following the passage of a bill that recognized DAOs as a legal entity in the state earlier this year. This makes Wyoming the first state in America to recognize and regulate DAOs, putting it at the forefront of the rapidly developing cryptocurrency industry. The approval of the American CryptoFed DAO is a significant milestone not just for Wyoming, but for the entire cryptocurrency industry. "The successful registration of the American CryptoFed DAO is a historic day for the blockchain industry in Wyoming and the United States," said Caitlin Long, CEO of Avanti Financial Group and a proponent of Wyoming's blockchain-friendly legislation. The American CryptoFed DAO's stablecoin, DAC, is set to launch later this year. Its approval marks a significant step towards the wider adoption and mainstream acceptance of cryptocurrencies as a viable form of payment and investment. The success of the DAO is sure to attract more investors and entrepreneurs, who will be looking to take advantage of Wyoming's supportive legal environment and robust blockchain ecosystem. In conclusion, the approval of America's first DAO in Wyoming signals a new era for blockchain technology and cryptocurrency regulation in America. It remains to be seen how this pioneering move will shape the future of the industry, but one thing is clear: Wyoming is leading the way.

You've probably noticed Whole30 on social media lately - it's more than just vegan food or paleo for those who know what they're doing... but most are not. In truth there's no right way to do it, since everyone has different needs and habits. But if you're contemplating going off your usual diet, here are some things to consider before giving up meat altogether... 1) Remember why you're starting! There are so many great reasons why we start a whole30 - weight loss (and even losing inches), improved digestion and health, feeling inspired after one day or two, improving our moods, building muscle energy levels, skincare benefits, etc. Make sure you choose a reason that's important enough to push yourself through every single challenge! 2) Think about how much easier life will be once you get started! When you're ready to stop eating foods from animal sources, all that's left to worry about is finding meals that satisfy your taste buds; however, when you're still consuming plenty of fruits and vegetables, it makes sense to mix it up and take advantage of already existing recipe ideas out there online. (Whole30 Recipes) 3) Be realistic! Plan ahead - try to make room in each meal plan for at least 3 days worth of "optional" treats throughout the week! (Let me give you an example!) Today my husband and I made homemade pasta salad for lunch as opposed to ordering pizza; tomorrow I'm planning to have green smoothies for breakfast instead of cereal bars and granola bar packets.... if I can keep these simple changes in mind now, I'll likely see improvements over the course of several weeks instead of months!!

Analysts attribute this sharp decline to the coronavirus pandemic, which has caused a significant drop in global demand for oil. With fewer cars, planes and ships in use, there is less need for fuel. In addition, OPEC countries have kept production levels relatively high despite the decreased demand, further driving down the price. This situation is likely to remain for some time. Many countries are still taking steps to limit the spread of COVID-19, such as travel restrictions, which will likely continue to adversely affect the demand for oil. For now, oil producers who rely heavily on oil revenue are feeling the pinch. Smaller countries, such as Venezuela and Nigeria, are particularly vulnerable. It remains to be seen how long oil prices will stay at these low levels. But if demand doesn't pick up soon, it could mean major consequences for the global economy.

The new bill, which would affect digital maps from Google, Apple, and Uber, is facing stiff opposition from campaign groups. It also bans "wrong" information, including disputed international borders. The EU law will force tech companies to delete this content from their maps, or face a fine of up to 20 million (23 million). One of the most controversial aspects of the bill is that it would allow countries to order tech companies to re-draw borders so they reflect their political point of view. This could lead to a situation where a country orders Google to change its maps so they show disputed territory as part of its own country. The bill doesn't say how tech companies would be expected to enforce these changes. The bill was put forward by the European Commission in October 2016, and is currently being considered by the European Parliament. It's not clear when it might become law. Opponents of the bill say it could lead to censorship, and would make it harder for people to find accurate information about the world. They also argue that it's not clear how the law would be enforced, and that it could lead to a race to the bottom, as countries compete to get tech companies to change their maps. The European Commission has said that the bill is necessary to protect people from misinformation, and that it would only apply to maps, not to other types of content, such as news articles.

The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) missed a deadline to name a squad for the tournament after the International Cricket Council (ICC) changed its revenue-sharing model. However, the national governing body has been given an extension until November 14. The ICC's revised model would benefit Test-playing nations financially, according to India Today. "We have received an email from the ICC saying that BCCI's submission will be considered by the ICC. The committee had given us a specific deadline of October 15 and we have not been given sufficient time to prepare the squad," board secretary Anurag Thakur told India Today. "We will be sending the squad on November 14." A 15-member squad must be submitted to the ICC by October 15. The BCCI is responsible for submitting the squad for the 2015 World Cup, which will take place in Australia and New Zealand from February 14. India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka are all in Group B and will begin the tournament on Feb. 15. India and Pakistan have never played in the World Cup tournament, while Sri Lanka has made it to the final four three times. The people of Cardiff Bay had come together to show their support for the French community and all those affected by the tragedy, and to reaffirm their commitment to building a more peaceful and tolerant world.

The Keep Military Museum in Dorchester plans to use the money to convert a bunker into an interactive experience. It also wants to create an online gallery of Dorset and New Forest troops killed in action in recent conflicts. The money will be used to cover the cost of the bunker conversion and the first year of the online gallery. The Keep Military Museum in Dorchester has been awarded 10,000 from the Big Lottery Fund. The money will be used to convert an underground bunker into an interactive experience, telling the story of the bunker, and what it was used for. It will also create an online gallery of Dorset and New Forest troops killed in action in recent conflicts. The museum already has a lot of information about the bunker, which was built to protect the town in the Second World War, but there are still several gaps in the knowledge. By working with The Keep Military Museum, volunteers will be able to help them to complete the story of the bunker and the role it played in Dorchester's history. The bunker and the online gallery will be finished in time for the 75th anniversary of the outbreak of the Second World War in 2015. Michael Eavis, Chairman of The Keep Military Museum, said: "We are thrilled to have won the Big Lottery Fund grant. It will help us to tell the story of the bunker and its use in the Second World War. We will also be able to put information about the lives of Dorset and New Forest troops killed in action in recent conflicts on line. It is a great project and we are very proud to have won this funding to help us bring it to fruition." The Big Lottery Fund distributes half of the money raised for good causes by the National Lottery.
